claim: 150 Swedish Arabidopsis thaliana accessions were grown at two different temperatures (10°C and 16°C).
source: To better understand how genotype and environment interact to affect DNA methylation and transcription, we grew 150 Arabidopsis thaliana accessions from Sweden (Long et al., 2013) in two different environments, 10°C and 16°C, chosen because they lead to very different flowering behavior (Atwell et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the experimental design involving 150 Swedish accessions grown at 10°C and 16°C.

claim: The growth temperatures of 10°C and 16°C were chosen because they lead to very different flowering behavior.
source: To better understand how genotype and environment interact to affect DNA methylation and transcription, we grew 150 Arabidopsis thaliana accessions from Sweden (Long et al., 2013) in two different environments, 10°C and 16°C, chosen because they lead to very different flowering behavior (Atwell et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites Atwell et al., 2010 as support for the temperature choice based on flowering behavior differences.

claim: In plants, DNA methylation occurs on cytosines in the CG, CHG, and CHH contexts.
source: In plants, DNA methylation occurs on cytosines in the CG, CHG, and CHH contexts (where H is any nucleotide except for C), each of which is catalyzed by independent pathways (Finnegan et al., 1998; Stroud et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites Finnegan et al., 1998 and Stroud et al., 2014 as support for this established knowledge about plant DNA methylation contexts.

claim: Each DNA methylation context (CG, CHG, CHH) is catalyzed by independent pathways.
source: In plants, DNA methylation occurs on cytosines in the CG, CHG, and CHH contexts (where H is any nucleotide except for C), each of which is catalyzed by independent pathways (Finnegan et al., 1998; Stroud et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites Finnegan et al., 1998 and Stroud et al., 2014 as support for independent methylation pathways.

claim: There is considerable variation in DNA methylation between accessions regardless of context.
source: Consistent with previous results (Vaughn et al., 2007; Eichten et al., 2013; Schmitz et al., 2013; Li et al., 2014; Seymour et al., 2014; Hagmann et al., 2015) we found considerable variation between accessions regardless of context, even at the level of genome-wide averages (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript presents data in Figure 1A and cites multiple previous studies supporting this observation.

claim: Temperature does not affect genome-wide CG methylation.
source: Temperature, on the other hand, did not appear to affect genome-wide CG or CHG methylation, but had a significant effect on CHH methylation, levels of which were 14% higher at 16°C than at 10°C, on average (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript presents data in Figure 1A showing no temperature effect on CG methylation.

claim: Temperature does not affect genome-wide CHG methylation.
source: Temperature, on the other hand, did not appear to affect genome-wide CG or CHG methylation, but had a significant effect on CHH methylation, levels of which were 14% higher at 16°C than at 10°C, on average (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript presents data in Figure 1A showing no temperature effect on CHG methylation.

claim: CHH methylation levels are 14% higher at 16°C than at 10°C on average.
source: Temperature, on the other hand, did not appear to affect genome-wide CG or CHG methylation, but had a significant effect on CHH methylation, levels of which were 14% higher at 16°C than at 10°C, on average (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative data showing a 14% increase in CHH methylation at higher temperature, supported by Figure 1A.

claim: No associations reached genome-wide significance for global CG methylation in GWAS.
source: For global CG and CHG methylation, no associations reached genome-wide significance, while for CHH methylation a clear peak of association was observed on chromosome 4 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports GWAS results showing no significant associations for CG methylation, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: No associations reached genome-wide significance for global CHG methylation in GWAS.
source: For global CG and CHG methylation, no associations reached genome-wide significance, while for CHH methylation a clear peak of association was observed on chromosome 4 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports GWAS results showing no significant associations for CHG methylation, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A clear peak of association was observed on chromosome 4 for CHH methylation in GWAS.
source: For global CG and CHG methylation, no associations reached genome-wide significance, while for CHH methylation a clear peak of association was observed on chromosome 4 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports GWAS results showing a significant association peak on chromosome 4, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: CHH methylation mostly occurs in transposons in Arabidopsis.
source: The association was even more significant when restricting attention to average CHH methylation of large transposons (Figure 1B), in agreement with the notion that this type of methylation mostly occurs in transposons in Arabidopsis (Stroud et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites Stroud et al., 2013 as support for CHH methylation occurring primarily in transposons.

claim: The association peak on chromosome 4 was even more significant when restricting attention to average CHH methylation of large transposons.
source: The association was even more significant when restricting attention to average CHH methylation of large transposons (Figure 1B), in agreement with the notion that this type of methylation mostly occurs in transposons in Arabidopsis (Stroud et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript presents GWAS data in Figure 1B showing stronger association when analyzing transposon methylation specifically.

claim: The association peak centers around a SNP at position 10,459,127 on chromosome 4.
source: The association centered around a SNP at 10,459,127 on chromosome 4, 38 kb downstream from the locus AT4G19020, which encodes a homolog of the CHG methyltransferase chromo-methylase-3 (Lindroth et al., 2001) that has recently been shown to catalyze both CHH and CHG methylation on transposons, and is thus an excellent candidate (Zemach et al., 2013; Stroud et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript reports the specific genomic position of the association peak from GWAS analysis.

claim: The SNP at 10,459,127 is 38 kb downstream from the locus AT4G19020.
source: The association centered around a SNP at 10,459,127 on chromosome 4, 38 kb downstream from the locus AT4G19020, which encodes a homolog of the CHG methyltransferase chromo-methylase-3 (Lindroth et al., 2001) that has recently been shown to catalyze both CHH and CHG methylation on transposons, and is thus an excellent candidate (Zemach et al., 2013; Stroud et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript reports the genomic distance between the SNP and the AT4G19020 locus.

claim: AT4G19020 encodes a homolog of the CHG methyltransferase chromo-methylase-3.
source: The association centered around a SNP at 10,459,127 on chromosome 4, 38 kb downstream from the locus AT4G19020, which encodes a homolog of the CHG methyltransferase chromo-methylase-3 (Lindroth et al., 2001) that has recently been shown to catalyze both CHH and CHG methylation on transposons, and is thus an excellent candidate (Zemach et al., 2013; Stroud et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites Lindroth et al., 2001 as support for the identity of AT4G19020 as a CMT3 homolog.

claim: CMT2 has been shown to catalyze both CHH and CHG methylation on transposons.
source: The association centered around a SNP at 10,459,127 on chromosome 4, 38 kb downstream from the locus AT4G19020, which encodes a homolog of the CHG methyltransferase chromo-methylase-3 (Lindroth et al., 2001) that has recently been shown to catalyze both CHH and CHG methylation on transposons, and is thus an excellent candidate (Zemach et al., 2013; Stroud et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites Zemach et al., 2013 and Stroud et al., 2014 as support for CMT2's catalytic activity.

claim: A multi-locus mixed model revealed another SNP downstream of CMT2 at position 10,454,628 (CMT2b).
source: A multi-locus mixed model (Segura et al., 2012) that included the identified SNP (CMT2a) as a fixed effect revealed another SNP downstream of CMT2, at position 10,454,628 (CMT2b), 4.5 kb closer to CMT2 than CMT2a, and in complete linkage disequilibrium with it (i.e., the non-reference alleles at CMT2a and CMT2b are never seen together).
evidence: The manuscript reports the discovery of a second SNP using multi-locus GWAS analysis.

claim: CMT2b is 4.5 kb closer to CMT2 than CMT2a.
source: A multi-locus mixed model (Segura et al., 2012) that included the identified SNP (CMT2a) as a fixed effect revealed another SNP downstream of CMT2, at position 10,454,628 (CMT2b), 4.5 kb closer to CMT2 than CMT2a, and in complete linkage disequilibrium with it (i.e., the non-reference alleles at CMT2a and CMT2b are never seen together).
evidence: The manuscript reports the relative genomic distances of the two SNPs to CMT2.

claim: CMT2a and CMT2b are in complete linkage disequilibrium.
source: A multi-locus mixed model (Segura et al., 2012) that included the identified SNP (CMT2a) as a fixed effect revealed another SNP downstream of CMT2, at position 10,454,628 (CMT2b), 4.5 kb closer to CMT2 than CMT2a, and in complete linkage disequilibrium with it (i.e., the non-reference alleles at CMT2a and CMT2b are never seen together).
evidence: The manuscript reports the linkage disequilibrium pattern between the two SNPs based on genetic data.

claim: The non-reference alleles at CMT2a and CMT2b are never seen together.
source: A multi-locus mixed model (Segura et al., 2012) that included the identified SNP (CMT2a) as a fixed effect revealed another SNP downstream of CMT2, at position 10,454,628 (CMT2b), 4.5 kb closer to CMT2 than CMT2a, and in complete linkage disequilibrium with it (i.e., the non-reference alleles at CMT2a and CMT2b are never seen together).
evidence: The manuscript reports the observed allele combinations in the population.

claim: Repeating GWAS with both CMT2a and CMT2b as cofactors identified no further loci.
source: Repeating the GWAS with both CMT2a and CMT2b as cofactors identified no further loci (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of a conditional GWAS analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both non-reference alleles at CMT2a and CMT2b are common in southern Sweden but also found in the north.
source: Both non-reference alleles are common in southern Sweden, but are also found in the north (22.6% vs 9.5% and 30.6% vs 7.9% for CMT2a and CMT2b, respectively).
evidence: The manuscript reports allele frequencies in different geographic regions.

claim: The non-reference CMT2a allele frequency is 22.6% in southern Sweden and 9.5% in northern Sweden.
source: Both non-reference alleles are common in southern Sweden, but are also found in the north (22.6% vs 9.5% and 30.6% vs 7.9% for CMT2a and CMT2b, respectively).
evidence: The manuscript reports specific allele frequencies for CMT2a in different regions.

claim: The non-reference CMT2b allele frequency is 30.6% in southern Sweden and 7.9% in northern Sweden.
source: Both non-reference alleles are common in southern Sweden, but are also found in the north (22.6% vs 9.5% and 30.6% vs 7.9% for CMT2a and CMT2b, respectively).
evidence: The manuscript reports specific allele frequencies for CMT2b in different regions.

claim: Accessions with the non-reference CMT2a allele have on average more CHH methylation on transposons than those with the reference haplotype (p = 1.1e-03).
source: Accessions with the non-reference CMT2a allele have on average more CHH methylation on transposons than those with the reference haplotype (p = 1.1e-03), while those with the non-reference CMT2b allele have lower levels of CHH methylation than the reference haplotype (p = 8.1e-03; Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of methylation differences between genotypes, shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Accessions with the non-reference CMT2b allele have lower levels of CHH methylation than the reference haplotype (p = 8.1e-03).
source: Accessions with the non-reference CMT2a allele have on average more CHH methylation on transposons than those with the reference haplotype (p = 1.1e-03), while those with the non-reference CMT2b allele have lower levels of CHH methylation than the reference haplotype (p = 8.1e-03; Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of methylation differences between genotypes, shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The associations between CMT2 alleles and CHH methylation were confirmed using an F2 population.
source: The associations were readily confirmed using an F2 population generated by crossing accessions with the CMT2a and CMT2b non-reference alleles (Figure 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports validation of the association using an independent F2 mapping population, shown in Figure 2.

claim: No significant differences in CMT2 mRNA levels were observed between the alleles.
source: No significant differences in CMT2 mRNA levels were observed between the alleles in our data and limited Sanger sequencing of cDNA showed no evidence of splicing variants (although, as will be discussed below, we did detect a putative rare null allele).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of gene expression data showing no expression differences between alleles.

claim: Limited Sanger sequencing of cDNA showed no evidence of splicing variants for CMT2.
source: No significant differences in CMT2 mRNA levels were observed between the alleles in our data and limited Sanger sequencing of cDNA showed no evidence of splicing variants (although, as will be discussed below, we did detect a putative rare null allele).
evidence: The manuscript reports Sanger sequencing results showing no splicing differences.

claim: A putative rare null allele of CMT2 was detected.
source: No significant differences in CMT2 mRNA levels were observed between the alleles in our data and limited Sanger sequencing of cDNA showed no evidence of splicing variants (although, as will be discussed below, we did detect a putative rare null allele).
evidence: The manuscript reports the detection of a rare null allele in the data.

claim: Several non-synonymous polymorphisms in the methyltransferase and BAH domains of CMT2 were detected.
source: Several non-synonymous polymorphisms in the methyltransferase and BAH domains of CMT2 were detected (Supplementary files 1 and 2) but they do not explain the phenotype as well as the CMT2a and CMT2b SNPs.
evidence: The manuscript reports detection of coding polymorphisms in CMT2 from sequence data.

claim: Non-synonymous polymorphisms in CMT2 do not explain the phenotype as well as the CMT2a and CMT2b SNPs.
source: Several non-synonymous polymorphisms in the methyltransferase and BAH domains of CMT2 were detected (Supplementary files 1 and 2) but they do not explain the phenotype as well as the CMT2a and CMT2b SNPs.
evidence: The manuscript reports comparative analysis of different polymorphisms' effects on the phenotype.

claim: 36,023 differentially methylated regions (DMRs) had at least one genome-wide significant association.
source: 36023 DMRs had at least one genome-wide significant association (Bonferroni-corrected p-value of 0.05; 7273 remain after correcting for multiple GWAS using an FDR of 0.05).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of significant associations from GWAS analysis of DMRs.

claim: 7,273 DMRs remain significant after correcting for multiple GWAS using an FDR of 0.05.
source: 36023 DMRs had at least one genome-wide significant association (Bonferroni-corrected p-value of 0.05; 7273 remain after correcting for multiple GWAS using an FDR of 0.05).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of DMRs remaining significant after multiple testing correction.

claim: 45% of DMRs with significant associations had a significant cis-association within 100 kb.
source: 45% (15,031) of the DMRs had a significant cis-association within 100 kb, while the rest showed evidence of trans-regulation, including the dramatic effect of CMT2 on chromosome 4 which accounted for approximately 21% (7392) of all significant associations (Figure 3A).
evidence: The manuscript reports the proportion of cis-associations from GWAS analysis, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CMT2 on chromosome 4 accounted for approximately 21% of all significant associations.
source: 45% (15,031) of the DMRs had a significant cis-association within 100 kb, while the rest showed evidence of trans-regulation, including the dramatic effect of CMT2 on chromosome 4 which accounted for approximately 21% (7392) of all significant associations (Figure 3A).
evidence: The manuscript reports the proportion of associations attributable to CMT2, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Variance-components analysis confirmed substantial cis and trans associations for CHH DMRs.
source: To quantify the regulation of DMRs, we partitioned the variance of CHH methylation into environmental (E), CMT2, CMT2 X E, cis, cis X E, trans, and trans X E using a mixed model (Figure 3B). The analysis confirmed substantial cis and trans associations, with the environment modulating the genetic effects rather than having a major direct effect.
evidence: The manuscript reports variance component analysis results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The environment modulates genetic effects on CHH methylation rather than having a major direct effect.
source: To quantify the regulation of DMRs, we partitioned the variance of CHH methylation into environmental (E), CMT2, CMT2 X E, cis, cis X E, trans, and trans X E using a mixed model (Figure 3B). The analysis confirmed substantial cis and trans associations, with the environment modulating the genetic effects rather than having a major direct effect.
evidence: The manuscript reports interpretation of variance component analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: SNPs may tag polymorphic TE insertions, with the insertion allele being silenced in a temperature-sensitive manner.
source: At least for the cis associations, a possible explanation is that SNPs tag polymorphic TE insertions, with the insertion allele being silenced in a temperature-sensitive manner.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a mechanistic explanation for the observed cis associations.

claim: Each accession on average gained CHH methylation at ~400 temperature DMRs when comparing 16°C to 10°C.
source: Comparing 16°C–10°C, each accession on average gained CHH methylation at ∼400 temperature DMRs and lost it at ∼200 temperature DMRs (false discovery rate = 0.05).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative analysis of temperature-dependent methylation changes.

claim: Each accession on average lost CHH methylation at ~200 temperature DMRs when comparing 16°C to 10°C.
source: Comparing 16°C–10°C, each accession on average gained CHH methylation at ∼400 temperature DMRs and lost it at ∼200 temperature DMRs (false discovery rate = 0.05).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative analysis of temperature-dependent methylation changes.

claim: CHH methylation is associated with transposable elements.
source: CHH methylation is associated with transposable elements (TEs; Finnegan et al., 1998), and in agreement with this, 79% of the temperature DMRs where methylation was gained at 16°C were located within 500 bp of an annotated TE (with 60% directly overlapping one).
evidence: The manuscript cites Finnegan et al., 1998 as support for the association between CHH methylation and TEs.

claim: 79% of temperature DMRs where methylation was gained at 16°C were located within 500 bp of an annotated TE.
source: CHH methylation is associated with transposable elements (TEs; Finnegan et al., 1998), and in agreement with this, 79% of the temperature DMRs where methylation was gained at 16°C were located within 500 bp of an annotated TE (with 60% directly overlapping one).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of the genomic location of temperature DMRs relative to TEs.

claim: 60% of temperature DMRs where methylation was gained at 16°C directly overlap an annotated TE.
source: CHH methylation is associated with transposable elements (TEs; Finnegan et al., 1998), and in agreement with this, 79% of the temperature DMRs where methylation was gained at 16°C were located within 500 bp of an annotated TE (with 60% directly overlapping one).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of the genomic overlap between temperature DMRs and TEs.

claim: Temperature DMRs were enriched in a small subset of 835 TEs (2.7% of total).
source: These temperature DMRs were enriched in a small subset of TEs (835, or 2.7% of total, permutation based p-value = 0.05) that were more highly methylated than other transposons, but with lower methylation levels immediately adjacent (Figure 4A).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of TE enrichment in temperature DMRs, shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Variable TEs were more highly methylated than other transposons but with lower methylation levels immediately adjacent.
source: These temperature DMRs were enriched in a small subset of TEs (835, or 2.7% of total, permutation based p-value = 0.05) that were more highly methylated than other transposons, but with lower methylation levels immediately adjacent (Figure 4A).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of methylation patterns in variable TEs, shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Variable TEs tend to be euchromatic compared to TEs without temperature DMRs.
source: Compared to TEs without temperature DMRs, these 'variable' TEs also tended to be euchromatic (Figure 4B), highly expressed (Figure 4C), and recently inserted ('evolutionarily young' TE insertions for which orthologs are not present in Arabidopsis lyrata [Zhong et al., 2012] comprised 75% of the variable TEs vs 68% of non-variable TEs).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of the genomic distribution of variable TEs, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Variable TEs tend to be highly expressed compared to TEs without temperature DMRs.
source: Compared to TEs without temperature DMRs, these 'variable' TEs also tended to be euchromatic (Figure 4B), highly expressed (Figure 4C), and recently inserted ('evolutionarily young' TE insertions for which orthologs are not present in Arabidopsis lyrata [Zhong et al., 2012] comprised 75% of the variable TEs vs 68% of non-variable TEs).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of TE expression levels, shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 75% of variable TEs are evolutionarily young insertions without orthologs in Arabidopsis lyrata, compared to 68% of non-variable TEs.
source: Compared to TEs without temperature DMRs, these 'variable' TEs also tended to be euchromatic (Figure 4B), highly expressed (Figure 4C), and recently inserted ('evolutionarily young' TE insertions for which orthologs are not present in Arabidopsis lyrata [Zhong et al., 2012] comprised 75% of the variable TEs vs 68% of non-variable TEs).
evidence: The manuscript reports comparative analysis of TE evolutionary age, citing Zhong et al., 2012 for the definition of young TEs.

claim: Members of the SINE, SINE-like, Helitrons and Mutator-like DNA TE superfamilies were over-represented among variable transposons.
source: At the super-family level, members of the SINE, SINE-like, Helitrons and Mutator-like DNA TE superfamilies were over-represented among the variable transposons, and at the family level, 36 families were over-represented, including the AtREP, Vandal and HAT DNA transposons, as well as COPIA78/ONSEN and META1 retroelements (Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports enrichment analysis of TE families among variable transposons, with results in Table 1.

claim: 36 TE families were over-represented among variable transposons, including AtREP, Vandal, HAT DNA transposons, COPIA78/ONSEN, and META1 retroelements.
source: At the super-family level, members of the SINE, SINE-like, Helitrons and Mutator-like DNA TE superfamilies were over-represented among the variable transposons, and at the family level, 36 families were over-represented, including the AtREP, Vandal and HAT DNA transposons, as well as COPIA78/ONSEN and META1 retroelements (Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports enrichment analysis of TE families, with detailed results in Table 1.

claim: COPIA78 has been shown to become active in response to heat stress.
source: Interestingly, COPIA78 has been shown to become active in response to heat stress (Pecinka et al., 2010; Ito et al., 2011) apparently due to heat-shock promoter elements in its LTR regions (Cavrak et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites Pecinka et al., 2010 and Ito et al., 2011 as support for COPIA78 heat stress activation.

claim: COPIA78 activation in response to heat stress is apparently due to heat-shock promoter elements in its LTR regions.
source: Interestingly, COPIA78 has been shown to become active in response to heat stress (Pecinka et al., 2010; Ito et al., 2011) apparently due to heat-shock promoter elements in its LTR regions (Cavrak et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites Cavrak et al., 2014 as support for the mechanism of COPIA78 heat stress activation.

claim: 10,138 DCL3-dependent DMRs were identified.
source: In order to gain further insight into the mechanisms responsible for variation in CHH methylation, we bisulfite-sequenced knockout lines of CMT2 (SAIL_906_G03) and DCL3 (dcl3-5 [Daxinger et al., 2009], a component of the RdDM pathway), and identified 10,138 DCL3-dependant DMRs and 33,422 CMT2-dependent DMRs as described in section 'DMR calling on DNA methylation mutants' of the 'Materials and methods'.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of DMRs identified from analysis of knockout mutants.

claim: 33,422 CMT2-dependent DMRs were identified.
source: In order to gain further insight into the mechanisms responsible for variation in CHH methylation, we bisulfite-sequenced knockout lines of CMT2 (SAIL_906_G03) and DCL3 (dcl3-5 [Daxinger et al., 2009], a component of the RdDM pathway), and identified 10,138 DCL3-dependant DMRs and 33,422 CMT2-dependent DMRs as described in section 'DMR calling on DNA methylation mutants' of the 'Materials and methods'.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of DMRs identified from analysis of knockout mutants.

claim: DCL3 is a component of the RdDM pathway.
source: In order to gain further insight into the mechanisms responsible for variation in CHH methylation, we bisulfite-sequenced knockout lines of CMT2 (SAIL_906_G03) and DCL3 (dcl3-5 [Daxinger et al., 2009], a component of the RdDM pathway), and identified 10,138 DCL3-dependant DMRs and 33,422 CMT2-dependent DMRs as described in section 'DMR calling on DNA methylation mutants' of the 'Materials and methods'.
evidence: The manuscript cites Daxinger et al., 2009 and states DCL3's role in the RdDM pathway as established knowledge.

claim: The GWAS peak at the CMT2 locus remains when considering only CMT2-dependent DMRs but not for DCL3-dependent DMRs.
source: As expected under the assumption that CMT2 is responsible for the massive GWAS peak on chromosome 4, the GWAS peak at this locus remains if we consider only the CMT2-dependent DMRs, but not for DCL3-dependent DMRs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports conditional GWAS results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: RNA silencing is less active at lower temperatures.
source: This result is consistent with previous findings showing that RNA silencing is less active at lower temperatures (Romon et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites Romon et al., 2013 as support for temperature effects on RNA silencing.

claim: One accession from northern Sweden (TAA-03) has almost undetectable levels of CHH methylation at CMT2-dependent DMRs.
source: Interestingly, we observed one accession from northern Sweden, TAA-03, with almost undetectable levels of CHH methylation at CMT2-dependant DMRs (Figure 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports observation of an outlier accession in the data, shown in Figure 5.

claim: TAA-03 has a deletion or rearrangement in CMT2.
source: Further investigation suggested that it has a deletion or rearrangement in CMT2, as we were unable to map reads between positions 2813 and 4944 (intron 7 to exon 16, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of sequencing read coverage indicating a structural variant, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Sanger sequencing indicates the insertion of a stretch of TC dinucleotide repeats of at least 330 bp in TAA-03.
source: Sanger-sequencing indicates the insertion of a stretch of TC dinucleotide repeats of at least 330 bp.
evidence: The manuscript reports Sanger sequencing results characterizing the structural variant.

claim: The same deletion in CMT2 appears to be present in three more accessions from northern Sweden (TAA-14, TAA-18, and Gro-3).
source: The same deletion appears to be present in three more accessions from northern Sweden (TAA-14, TAA-18, and Gro-3) a situation reminiscent of the homologous CMT1 gene, which seems to be non-functional in most Arabidopsis accessions (Henikoff and Comai, 1998).
evidence: The manuscript reports identification of the same deletion in additional accessions.

claim: CMT1 seems to be non-functional in most Arabidopsis accessions.
source: The same deletion appears to be present in three more accessions from northern Sweden (TAA-14, TAA-18, and Gro-3) a situation reminiscent of the homologous CMT1 gene, which seems to be non-functional in most Arabidopsis accessions (Henikoff and Comai, 1998).
evidence: The manuscript cites Henikoff and Comai, 1998 as support for CMT1 being non-functional in most accessions.

claim: CMT2 null alleles have no obvious phenotype.
source: Although CMT2 null alleles have no obvious phenotype, the gene is highly conserved in plants (with the exception of maize; Zemach et al., 2013; West et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript states the lack of obvious phenotype for CMT2 null alleles based on observation.

claim: CMT2 is highly conserved in plants with the exception of maize.
source: Although CMT2 null alleles have no obvious phenotype, the gene is highly conserved in plants (with the exception of maize; Zemach et al., 2013; West et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites Zemach et al., 2013 and West et al., 2014 as support for CMT2 conservation patterns.

claim: Natural variation in CMT2 has been suggested to be associated with adaptation to climate.
source: It has recently been suggested that natural variation in CMT2 is associated with adaptation to climate (Shen et al., 2014), although the alleles identified in that study do not overlap with the ones identified here.
evidence: The manuscript cites Shen et al., 2014 as proposing a link between CMT2 variation and climate adaptation.

claim: The alleles identified by Shen et al., 2014 do not overlap with the ones identified in this study.
source: It has recently been suggested that natural variation in CMT2 is associated with adaptation to climate (Shen et al., 2014), although the alleles identified in that study do not overlap with the ones identified here.
evidence: The manuscript compares the alleles identified in this study with those from Shen et al., 2014.

claim: CHH methylation was moderately correlated with photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) in spring (Pearson's r = 0.38).
source: While CHH methylation was moderately correlated with photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) in spring (Pearson's r = 0.38), and CHG showed correlation with aridity (r = 0.35) and the number of frost-free days (Pearson's r = 0.30), by far the strongest signal was a strong positive correlation between CG methylation and latitude (Pearson's r = 0.70), as well as with a number of environmental variables that co-vary with latitude in our sample, such as minimum temperature and daytime length (Table 2, Figure 6A).
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis between methylation and environmental variables, with detailed results in Table 2.

claim: CHG methylation showed correlation with aridity (r = 0.35).
source: While CHH methylation was moderately correlated with photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) in spring (Pearson's r = 0.38), and CHG showed correlation with aridity (r = 0.35) and the number of frost-free days (Pearson's r = 0.30), by far the strongest signal was a strong positive correlation between CG methylation and latitude (Pearson's r = 0.70), as well as with a number of environmental variables that co-vary with latitude in our sample, such as minimum temperature and daytime length (Table 2, Figure 6A).
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis between methylation and environmental variables, with detailed results in Table 2.

claim: CHG methylation showed correlation with the number of frost-free days (Pearson's r = 0.30).
source: While CHH methylation was moderately correlated with photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) in spring (Pearson's r = 0.38), and CHG showed correlation with aridity (r = 0.35) and the number of frost-free days (Pearson's r = 0.30), by far the strongest signal was a strong positive correlation between CG methylation and latitude (Pearson's r = 0.70), as well as with a number of environmental variables that co-vary with latitude in our sample, such as minimum temperature and daytime length (Table 2, Figure 6A).
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis between methylation and environmental variables, with detailed results in Table 2.

claim: There is a strong positive correlation between CG methylation and latitude (Pearson's r = 0.70).
source: While CHH methylation was moderately correlated with photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) in spring (Pearson's r = 0.38), and CHG showed correlation with aridity (r = 0.35) and the number of frost-free days (Pearson's r = 0.30), by far the strongest signal was a strong positive correlation between CG methylation and latitude (Pearson's r = 0.70), as well as with a number of environmental variables that co-vary with latitude in our sample, such as minimum temperature and daytime length (Table 2, Figure 6A).

claim: CG methylation is correlated with environmental variables that co-vary with latitude, such as minimum temperature and daytime length.
source: While CHH methylation was moderately correlated with photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) in spring (Pearson's r = 0.38), and CHG showed correlation with aridity (r = 0.35) and the number of frost-free days (Pearson's r = 0.30), by far the strongest signal was a strong positive correlation between CG methylation and latitude (Pearson's r = 0.70), as well as with a number of environmental variables that co-vary with latitude in our sample, such as minimum temperature and daytime length (Table 2, Figure 6A).
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis with multiple environmental variables, detailed in Table 2.

claim: Accessions from northern Sweden (minimum temperature below −10°C) had on average 11% higher global CG methylation compared to those from the south.
source: As a result of the strong latitudinal correlation, accessions originating from northern Sweden (minimum temperature below −10°C) had on average 11% higher global CG methylation compared to those from the south (Figure 6A).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative comparison of methylation levels between geographic regions, shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The correlation between CG methylation and latitude appears to be driven by gene body methylation (GBM).
source: The correlation appears to be driven by gene body methylation (GBM): as the correlation for CG methylation on transposons was much weaker (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript infers the source of the correlation by comparing methylation patterns in different genomic features, shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The correlation for CG methylation on transposons was much weaker than for gene body methylation.
source: The correlation appears to be driven by gene body methylation (GBM): as the correlation for CG methylation on transposons was much weaker (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports comparative analysis of methylation correlations in different genomic features, shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Genes were classified into 'unmethylated' and 'having GBM' using a cutoff of 5% average CG methylation.
source: Because the methylation variation observed for genes with average CG methylation below 5% appeared mostly to be noise (Figure 6—figure supplement 2, see also the 'Materials and methods' section), we classified genes into 'unmethylated' and 'having GBM' using this as a cutoff (5%).
evidence: The manuscript describes the classification method used for defining GBM genes, with supporting data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Genes showing a transposon-like pattern of methylation (high CG, CHH, and CHG methylation) were eliminated from GBM analysis.
source: We also eliminated genes showing a transposon-like pattern of methylation in which not only CG, but also the CHH and CHG contexts are highly methylated (Zemach et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript describes filtering criteria for GBM analysis, citing Zemach et al., 2013 for the definition of transposon-like methylation.

claim: Methylation was detectable at a similar number of CG sites in the north and south (1,085,292 vs 1,079,443 CG sites).
source: Although methylation was detectable (using a cut-off of 1%) at a similar number of sites in the north and south (1085292 vs 1079443 CG sites), those in the north showed a distinct skew towards higher methylation levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative analysis of methylated sites in different geographic regions, shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: CG sites in the north showed a distinct skew towards higher methylation levels compared to the south.
source: Although methylation was detectable (using a cut-off of 1%) at a similar number of sites in the north and south (1085292 vs 1079443 CG sites), those in the north showed a distinct skew towards higher methylation levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of methylation level distributions shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: The majority of cytosines in GBM genes showed a small increase in methylation in the north compared to the south.
source: Likewise when the difference between average methylation levels in the north and south was calculated individually for each of the cytosines, the majority of cytosines showed a small increase in the north compared to the south (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of per-cytosine methylation differences shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: There is a general small increase in methylation of most CG dinucleotides in GBM genes in the north, rather than large changes in a specific subset.
source: From this we concluded that there is a general small increase in methylation of most CG dinucleotides in GBM genes, rather than large changes in a specific subset.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the analysis of per-cytosine methylation differences.

claim: GBM primarily occurs on long, evolutionary conserved genes that tend to be moderately-to-highly expressed.
source: GBM primarily occurs on long, evolutionary conserved genes that tend to be moderately-to-highly expressed, and is positively correlated with gene expression (Zilberman et al., 2007; Takuno and Gaut, 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites Zilberman et al., 2007 and Takuno and Gaut, 2012 as support for the characteristics of GBM genes.

claim: GBM is positively correlated with gene expression.

claim: Genes with higher GBM tended to be more highly expressed in the data.
source: Genes with higher GBM tended to be more highly expressed in our data as well, and—more interestingly—accessions with higher average GBM showed slightly higher average expression of methylated genes (although the correlation was weak, Figure 6—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of the relationship between GBM and expression in their data, shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5.

claim: Accessions with higher average GBM showed slightly higher average expression of methylated genes.
source: Genes with higher GBM tended to be more highly expressed in our data as well, and—more interestingly—accessions with higher average GBM showed slightly higher average expression of methylated genes (although the correlation was weak, Figure 6—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of the relationship between GBM and expression across accessions, shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5.

claim: Genes with GBM were on average more highly expressed in northern than in southern accessions.

claim: Unmethylated genes showed little expression difference between northern and southern accessions.

claim: GBM has been shown to be anti-correlated with temperature-dependent gene expression.
source: GBM has previously been shown to be anti-correlated with temperature-dependent gene expression (Kumar and Wigge, 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites Kumar and Wigge, 2010 as support for the relationship between GBM and temperature-dependent expression.

claim: Northern accessions showed considerably less variation in expression between 10°C and 16°C for genes with GBM (Wilcoxon p-value = 1.2e-05).
source: While no large-scale north-south expression differences were observed between 10°C and 16°C in our data, northern accessions showed considerably less variation in expression between the two temperatures for genes with GBM (Wilcoxon p-value = 1.2e-05), while no such difference was observed for genes without it (Figure 6—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of expression variation between temperatures, shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 6.

claim: No difference in expression variation between temperatures was observed for genes without GBM between northern and southern accessions.

evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of expression variation between temperatures, shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 6.

claim: Variance-component analysis revealed that trans effects for GBM are massive relative to CHH methylation.
source: As for CHH DMRs, the genetic basis of GBM was examined using a variance-component approach (Figure 7A). The results were dramatically different: relative to CHH methylation, the trans effects for GBM are massive, and the environment appears to have no effect (in agreement with the observation that only CHH methylation levels vary with temperature, see Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript reports variance component analysis results shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The environment appears to have no effect on GBM.

source: A comparison of the direction of the effect of GBM-associated SNPs in cis and trans revealed a striking pattern (Figure 7C). While the non-reference alleles of cis-SNPs were 1.18 times more likely to be associated with decreased rather than increased GBM (p = 2.01e-04), the non-reference alleles of trans-SNPs were 3.48 times more likely to be associated with increased GBM (p = 2.2e-16), and the non-reference alleles at the 15 trans-SNPs that were associated with GBM at five or more genes were always positively correlated (Figure 7C).

source: The 15 SNPs were more than ninefold over-represented in the previously identified sweep regions (empirical p-value = 5.1e-03) and over fivefold over-represented within 2 kb of SNPs in the 1% tail of those associated with minimum temperature (Hancock et al., 2011) (empirical p-value = 3.1e-04), (Table 3).

claim: The north vs south divide explains a much higher fraction of the additive genetic variance for GBM (Qst = 0.772) than of the SNP variance (Fst = 0.187).

The north vs south divide explains a much higher fraction of the additive genetic variance for GBM (Qst = 0.772; see 'Materials and methods') than of the SNP variance (Fst = 0.187).

claim: 68 genes within 100 kB of one of the 15-trans SNPs have expression highly correlated with the adjacent SNP after correction for population structure (Wilcoxon test p < 0.001).

claim: The increased gene-body methylation observed in the north may not be directly due to increased DNA methylation, but may be caused by increases in gene expression driven by differences in transcription factor networks or chromatin compaction.
source: This may suggest that the increased gene-body methylation observed in the north is not directly due to increased DNA methylation, but may be caused by increases in gene expression driven either by differences in transcription factors networks or chromatin compaction.

claim: Local adaptation in A. thaliana involves genome-wide changes in fundamental mechanisms of gene regulation.
source: In conclusion, genes with GBM are generally up-regulated and more heavily methylated in northern accessions, and the change appears to be due to trans-acting polymorphisms that have been subject to directional selection. The candidate regions show an overrepresentation of genes involved in transcriptional processes. We also found that CHH methylation of TEs is temperature sensitive, and identified a major trans-acting controller, CMT2. Taken together, these observations suggest that local adaptation in A. thaliana involves genome-wide changes in fundamental mechanisms of gene regulation, perhaps as a form of temperature compensation.
evidence: The manuscript synthesizes multiple lines of evidence to propose this conclusion about local adaptation.

claim: The genome-wide changes in gene regulation may represent a form of temperature compensation.
